description: We are 6th graders, excited space explorers.
summary:
An interactive 3D time-travel experience that introduces school-age space enthusiasts to the hardware NASA has left across the solar system. Built as a single HTML file with Three.js, it places users in a time-machine cockpit where they pick a date or press "Surprise Me." A wormhole sequence carries them to one of 14 real events, from Surveyor 3 on the Moon (1967) to Ingenuity on Mars (2021), including Voyager 1 in interstellar space and lost craft such as Mars Polar Lander.

  At each destination, a 3D model of the machine tells its own story in four chapters: why it was sent, its journey, what it discovered, and where it is today. Animations show the science in action, such as a laser bouncing off the Apollo 11 retroreflector. Users can return to the time machine at any time.

  Dense mission archives rarely reach young audiences. By turning silent machines into narrators, it links engineering to discovery and builds a personal connection to exploration. Keyboard navigation, reduced-motion and text-only modes, and two reading levels make it accessible to more learners.
details:
What it does and how it works

Chrono-Probe is a browser-based 3D time-travel story about the hardware NASA has left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space.

  1. Time Machine Hub: users start in an animated cockpit. They can enter a date, press "Surprise Me" for a random event, or pick one of 14 events on a timeline dial. If the date doesn't match an event, the closest event is chosen.
  2. Time travel: the camera rushes through a wormhole while a date counter rolls back to the target year.
  3. Destination: users arrive in a 3D scene that matches where the hardware is today:
    • the grey surface of the Moon, with Earth on the horizon
    • the rust-red plains of Mars
    • the starfield of deep space
    • a fog-covered "Location Unknown" scene for lost craft such as Mars Polar Lander and Apollo 10's "Snoopy"
  4. Story: a 3D model of the machine tells its own story in four chapters: Why I Was Sent, The Journey, What I Discovered and Where I Am Today. Each chapter starts an animation, such as a laser hitting the Apollo 11 retroreflector, Phoenix digging up ice, or Ingenuity taking off.
  5. Return: a button (or the Esc key) brings users back to the time machine at any time. A Journey Log tracks which events they've explored.

Benefits

  • Shows instead of lists: users watch how each machine worked rather than reading facts.
  • Links engineering to discovery: every story connects a piece of hardware to what it taught us.
  • Lets users explore freely: the date picker and random option give each visit a different path.
  • Easy to run: it's a single HTML file with no install, so it works on classroom computers, Chromebooks and tablets.

Intended impact

  • Help young people see the machines behind today's missions, not just the active ones.
  • Build a personal connection to these machines, so they're remembered as explorers rather than abandoned equipment.
  • Show the human side: Sojourner and Ingenuity were named by students, which tells young users they can take part too.
  • Give teachers a ready-made, accurate resource for science and history lessons.

Tools and technologies

Area

Tools

Languages

HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES modules)

3D graphics

Three.js (WebGL), OrbitControls, UnrealBloomPass (glow effect)

Visuals

Textures and shaders generated in code; models built from simple 3D shapes, so no external files are needed

Animation

A custom easing helper, requestAnimationFrame

Data

NASA mission facts stored in a JSON-style list (check against the challenge Resources)

Development

Enchanté AI assistant on macOS, any modern browser

Hardware

A standard laptop; runs on desktop, tablet and phone

What makes it creative

  • Time travel as the way in: users choose a date and are taken to the place where history happened, so it feels like an adventure rather than a lesson.
  • Machines tell their own stories: silent rovers and probes speak in the first person, clearly marked as imagined narration.
  • Lost hardware is part of the story: missing craft get their own "Location Unknown" scene, which shows that exploration includes failure and mystery.
  • Random discovery: "Surprise Me" makes it fun to come back again.

What we considered

  • Accuracy: only verified facts are used, imagined quotes are labeled as such (for example, Opportunity's "my battery is low" was a reporter's summary, not a message the rover sent), status is clearly marked, and only NASA hardware is included.
  • Age range: two reading levels, "Explorer" (ages 8–10) and "Scientist" (ages 11–14).
  • Accessibility:
    • full keyboard navigation and screen-reader labels
    • story text in real HTML, not drawn on the 3D canvas
    • a reduced-motion setting that follows the device preference
    • WCAG AA color contrast
    • a text-only mode if the device doesn't support WebGL
  • Performance: aims for 60 fps; unused 3D objects are cleaned up between scenes; nothing large to load.
  • Representation: includes the people behind the missions, such as Dr. George Carruthers and the student namers Valerie Ambroise and Vaneeza Rupani.
  • Range of stories: covers active, silent and lost hardware across the Moon, Mars and deep space, from 1967 to 2021.
